result:
I reviewed the actual diff and live-reproduced the intended fix scenario rather than trusting the self-report. Verdict: **reject**.

The core fix (the `ambiguous` flag distinguishing "gh confirmed not-merged" from "gh call itself failed") is sound and its test passes. But reproducing the exact scenario `--audit-plans` exists for — two phases in the same plan file both falsely self-reporting done — exposed a real bug: reverting the first violation can delete lines from the on-disk file (when the parent state lacked `completed_by_task`/`evidence`), which shifts line numbers for later blocks in the same file. `blame_line()` then blames the shifted line number against `git blame HEAD` (HEAD still reflects the pre-revert, larger file), landing on the wrong commit. In my repro this produced a corrupted hash (a stray `^` boundary-commit marker), aborted the second phase's revert with a bogus "parent could not be read" incident, left that phase's false self-report un-reverted, and still auto-committed + pushed the (correct) first revert plus the corrupted incident text to master.

No test in the suite covers more than one violation per file, so this shipped despite 10 passing scenarios. Given this is tier1 (autonomous merge) and the bug hits exactly the multi-violation case the feature is meant to handle, I wrote a reject verdict with details to `review-verdict.json`.
